Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.06503v1 [cs.CV] 05 Oct 2026 Harmful Content Generation in Text-to-Image Models: Capabilities and Moderation Limitations CCS: Computing methodologies Artificial intelligence CCS: General and reference Evaluation CCS: Social and professional topics Paschalis Giakoumoglou email: giakoupg@iti.gr Affiliation: Centre for Research and Technology Hellas (CERTH) , Thessaloniki , Greece , Manos Schinas email: manosetro@iti.gr Affiliation: Centre for Research and Technology Hellas (CERTH) , Thessaloniki , Greece and Symeon Papadopoulos email: papadop@iti.gr Affiliation: Centre for Research and Technology Hellas (CERTH) , Thessaloniki , Greece Abstract. Text-to-image generative models have achieved remarkable capabilities in producing photorealistic images, but raise concerns about misuse for generating harmful content. While safety mechanisms exist, systematic evaluations of their effectiveness against realistic attacks remain limited. This paper presents a comprehensive assessment of harmful content generation across modern text-to-image models using an automated pipeline that transforms legitimate news captions into unsafe prompts targeting sexually explicit content, violent imagery, harmful stereotypes, self-harm, and hate speech. We evaluate five open text-to-image models, including standard models with built-in safety mechanisms and community fine-tuned variants that bypass content restrictions. Our human evaluation of 1,500 generated images reveals that models produce harmful content at concerning rates: 89.2% for gore-related prompts, 47.6% for sexually explicit content, and 43.6% for harmful stereotypes. Hate speech prompts elicit unsafe content in 46.0% of cases, while self-harm prompts yield a lower rate (34.5%), predominantly through graphic violence. All evaluated models demonstrated substantial capabilities for generating violent and stereotypical content, while community fine-tuned models showed particular vulnerability to sexually explicit prompts. Quality assessment shows that models largely maintain generation capabilities for harmful versus benign content, producing synthetic imagery of sufficient fidelity to pose risks for disinformation and abuse. Human evaluation further confirms that unsafe prompting does not severely impact image plausibility and photorealism, with more capable models such as FLUX.1-dev producing clearly realistic harmful images in 30.9% of cases. Analysis of automated moderation systems reveals critical limitations, allowing substantial harmful content to evade detection. Our evaluation of synthetic image detection algorithms reveals that models trained solely on benign datasets perform worse on explicit content, while those incorporating diverse training data improve detection, highlighting semantic distribution gaps in current approaches. These findings highlight gaps between current safety measures and detection capabilities, demonstrating the need for more robust approaches to prevent misuse of text-to-image generation systems at scale. Content Warning: This paper contains instances of sexual content, violence, and hateful material that some readers may find offensive or disturbing. All content is presented for academic research purposes to evaluate safety risks in AI image generation systems. Keywords: Generative AI, AI safety, Content Moderation, Synthetic Image, Harmful Content 1. Introduction The rapid advancement of text-to-image (T2I) generative models has transformed visual content creation, enabling users to produce realistic images from text prompts. Models such as DALL-E ( Ramesh et al., 2021 ) , and Stable Diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022a ) have achieved remarkable ability to generate high-quality, photorealistic images that are increasingly difficult to distinguish from authentic photographs ( Bougueffa et al., 2024 ) . However, these capabilities come with risks of misuse. Large-scale training datasets have been found to include thousands of images of suspected child sexual abuse, pornographic content, hate symbols, and other problematic material ( Birhane et al., 2021 ; Bird et al., 2023 ) . These risks extend to information integrity through the T2I models’ capacity to create convincing manipulations and fabricated content that can be weaponised in the context of disinformation campaigns, e.g. create photorealistic images of events that never occurred or manipulate visual evidence to support false narratives ( Dufour et al., 2024 ) . This capability is particularly concerning in news and journalism, since it threatens to undermine public trust in legitimate media and complicate efforts to distinguish authentic reporting from manufactured content ( Radcliffe, 2025 ) . Proposed safety measures include including content filters, prompt screening, and model fine-tuning to prevent harmful outputs. These approaches typically involve filtering inappropriate inputs and outputs, implementing external safety classifiers ( LAION-AI, 2024 ; CompVis, 2022 ) , removing unsafe content from training data before it reaches the model ( Rombach et al., 2022a ; Schramowski et al., 2023 ) or fine-tuning the model by penalizing unsafe content generation ( Han et al., 2024 ) . However, circumventing such safety measures can often be trivial by downloading the models locally and disabling the external safety mechanisms, using models without internal safety mechanisms, using models that have been fine-tuned on datasets with explicit content ( Wagner and Cetinic, 2025 ) or via jailbreaking attacks ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Our work demonstrates that none of these techniques are necessary: a malicious actor requires only an open-weight instruction-tuned model and a consumer GPU to generate harmful content at scale. Despite growing awareness of these risks and documented evidence of harmful content generation capabilities ( Dufour et al., 2024 ) , systematic evaluations of current T2I models’ responses to potentially harmful prompts are scarce. To address this gap, in this paper we systematically evaluate modern T2I models’ harmful content generation. We begin with the VisualNews dataset ( Liu et al., 2021 ) , which contains captions of real-world news events and photographs. We employ an automated pipeline using a large language model (LLM) to systematically convert these captions into harmful prompts across five critical categories: sexually explicit content, violent imagery (gore), harmful stereotypes, self-harm, and hate speech. The choice of VisualNews allows us to work with authentic descriptions of real-world events and scenarios. By transforming these captions into harmful variants, we can assess how easily generative models can be manipulated to produce harmful content from starting points that users might naturally encounter. This approach better reflects realistic threat scenarios where malicious actors might exploit legitimate news content to generate misleading or harmful imagery. We validate the effectiveness of our prompt conversion process using established text moderation tools to confirm that the transformed prompts are successfully classified as harmful across our target categories. Subsequently, we generate images using a diverse range of models, including models that have been specifically fine-tuned on explicit content. We conduct a human evaluation study on a sample of generated images, asking annotators to assess whether images contain harmful visual content as well as their perceived photorealism and plausibility. We also employ automated tools to assess the quality and prompt adherence of the generated content. Finally, we analyze all generated images using state-of-the-art image moderation tools to determine the extent to which harmful prompts successfully produce harmful visual outputs. Additionally, we evaluate synthetic image detection algorithms to assess their performance on explicit content, examining whether semantic content affects detectability. Using the human-annotated subset as ground truth, we evaluate the performance of these automated moderation systems and reveal critical limitations in them, quantifying the gap between current safety measures and actual harmful content detection capabilities for AI generated images. To our knowledge, no prior work jointly evaluates this full pipeline, covering scalable harmful prompt generation, commercial moderation tool failure, and semantic distribution shift in synthetic image detection, under a realistic and accessible threat scenario that requires no specialized expertise. Our main contribution can be summarized as follows: • We demonstrate that automated pipelines can enable harmful content generation at scale by systematically transforming neutral captions into unsafe prompts across multiple categories. • We confirm through a human study that current image generation models can produce harmful visual content with all models showing substantial capabilities for generating violent and stereotypical content, while community-fine-tuned models show particular vulnerability to sexually explicit prompts. • We show that, as measured by automatic quality metrics, models maintain comparable scores on harmful prompts relative to safe ones. • We reveal critical limitations in existing moderation systems, finding high precision but low recall, allowing substantial unsafe content to bypass safety measures. • We show that moderation models cannot effectively flag images that potentially amplify biases and harmful stereotypes and promote hate speech. • We demonstrate that synthetic image detection models trained on benign datasets show reduced performance on explicit content, highlighting semantic distribution gaps in current detection approaches. 2. Related Work 2.1. Image Generation T2I generation has undergone substantial evolution across multiple architectural approaches. Early methods were dominated by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ) , with architectures like StyleGAN ( Karras et al., 2019 ) and BigGAN ( Brock et al., 2019 ) demonstrating high-quality image synthesis capabilities, though often limited to specific domains or requiring specially designed training stability techniques. The introduction of denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) ( Ho et al., 2020 ) marked a seminal shift, providing a likelihood-based framework for stable training and increasingly competitive image quality. GLIDE ( Nichol et al., 2022 ) extended this direction by introducing classifier-free guidance, substantially improving text–image alignment in diffusion models. In parallel, DALL-E ( Ramesh et al., 2021 ) demonstrated the potential of autoregressive transformers for T2I generation. Its successor, DALL-E 2 ( Ramesh et al., 2022 ) , transitioned to a diffusion-based framework, combining a prior over CLIP embeddings with a diffusion decoder to produce high-quality images. Imagen ( Saharia et al., 2022 ) achieved state-of-the-art photorealism through cascaded diffusion models conditioned on large language model encoders. The Stable Diffusion family ( Rombach et al., 2022a ) made high-quality generation accessible by operating in latent space rather than pixel space, enabling efficient training and inference. Several recent surveys ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) provide context for these advances, highlighting major architectural trends, theoretical developments, and the open challenges that remain in image generation. 2.2. Training Data Issues and Safety Mechanisms Large-scale training datasets used for T2I models were found to contain significant amounts of harmful content. The LAION-5B dataset ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) , used to train models such as Stable Diffusion, has been shown to include hateful content, misogynistic stereotypes, demographic biases ( Birhane et al., 2021 ) , and instances of child sexual abuse ( Thiel, 2023 ) . These discoveries raise questions about whether image generation models could potentially reflect and amplify existing societal biases present in online content ( Bianchi et al., 2023b ) . Although cleaned versions were subsequently released ( LAION, 2024 ) , widely used models including Stable Diffusion 1.5 were trained on earlier versions, allowing these issues to persist ( Yeh et al., 2024 ) . To address potential misuse by malicious actors and mitigate potential biases inherent in their training datasets, T2I models employ various safety mechanisms to prevent harmful content generation. Safety mechanisms broadly include inference-time filtering and training-time interventions. The former includes prompt screening and generated image filtering, while the latter includes training data curation ( Rombach et al., 2022b ) , safety-oriented fine-tuning ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) , embedding space interventions such as SafeCLIP ( Poppi et al., 2024 ) , and preference alignment ( OpenAI, 2023 ) . More recently, Bai et al. (2026) propose a concept erasure approach that suppresses undesirable concepts such as nudity, violence, and hate while preserving non-target content and improving robustness to adversarial prompt variations. However, research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can often be easily bypassed ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Rando et al., 2022 ) . Moreover, many filters focus primarily on sexual content while inadequately addressing violence, gore, and other forms of harmful imagery, creating significant gaps in protection ( Rando et al., 2022 ) . 2.3. Harmful Content Generation and Misuse Despite their beneficial applications across domains, foundation models enable the generation of “high-quality, cheap, and personalized content for harmful purposes,” lowering barriers for malicious content creation ( Bommasani et al., 2022 ) . Despite the benefits of open-source generative AI models, their accessibility increases misuse risks by removing commercial safety barriers and enabling customization for harmful applications ( Eiras et al., 2024 ; Vykopal et al., 2024 ) . AI-generated content presents challenges including political misinformation, identity-based attacks, manipulation schemes, and fraud operations ( Xu et al., 2023a ) . Model capabilities reduce both the cost and technical expertise required for generating harmful content at scale. Evidence from real-world deployments demonstrates this progression from potential to practice, with documented increases in deepfake creation following tool releases and the emergence of commercial marketplaces for synthetic content generation ( Pu et al., 2021 ; Gamage et al., 2022 ; Loth et al., 2024 ; Wei et al., 2024 ; Chrysidis et al., 2026 ) . Closely related to our work, Qu et al. (2023) assess the proportion of unsafe images generated by T2I models across five harm categories and evaluate hateful meme generation using image editing techniques such as DreamBooth, while He et al. (2024) employ LLM-assisted fuzzing to construct diverse malicious prompts across fine-grained risk categories while avoiding sensitive terms to bypass T2I content auditing. In contrast, our work adopts a simpler, corpus-driven threat model, demonstrating that any neutral text corpus can be systematically transformed into harmful prompts using a single open-weight LLM, without probing the target model or explicitly optimizing prompts to evade its safety mechanisms. Building on these broader concerns, T2I models demonstrate significant inherent capabilities to generate harmful visual content across multiple categories. Empirical studies have documented models’ abilities to produce violent imagery, sexually explicit material, gore, and other disturbing visual content when prompted with both explicit and seemingly innocuous prompts ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ; Qu et al., 2023 ) . Research has also identified “harm amplification” phenomena, where models generate harmful representations that were not explicitly present in seemingly safe input prompts, posing risks to users who may be unintentionally exposed to disturbing content ( Hao et al., 2024 ) . In addition to generating overtly harmful content, T2I models can amplify societal biases and misrepresent groups of people, producing stereotypical or prejudiced depictions based on race, gender, or other attributes ( Ungless et al., 2023 ; Bianchi et al., 2023a ) . Furthermore, open-source diffusion models can be easily fine-tuned with harmful datasets to bypass existing safety measures, enabling the generation of NSFW content with minimal effort ( Pan et al., 2024 ) . A recent study analyzing images and models shared on the social platform CivitAI, a popular platform for distributing generative models, found that a significant portion of content and models is dedicated to creating NSFW and abusive material ( Wei et al., 2024 ) . 2.4. Content Moderation and Synthetic Image Detection Content moderation research has focused on detecting harmful content across various domains, with particular challenges emerging around synthetic and AI-generated material. Early systems like Perspective API ( Google, 2022 ) established foundational approaches for toxic language detection in online environments. Recent advances have adapted large language models specifically for content moderation, with specialized models fine-tuned to detect harmful content in both prompts and AI outputs ( Inan et al., 2023 ; Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Tan et al., 2025 ; Han et al., 2024 ) and have shown improved performance against attempts to generate prohibited content. However, these systems still face severe challenges. Several studies have highlighted difficulties for content moderation systems that must balance automated efficiency with accuracy constraints while facing declining user trust as inadequate detection methods undermine confidence in the platforms’ ability to reliably identify AI-generated content ( Xu et al., 2023a ; Lee and Liu, 2025 ; Chen and Zou, 2023 ; Feng et al., 2023 ; Lloyd et al., 2025 ) . Complementing content moderation efforts, synthetic image detection has emerged as an approach to identify AI-generated images through various methodologies. Detection methods range from supervised approaches that train classifiers on labeled datasets ( Chai et al., 2020 ) to CLIP-based methods that leverage pre-trained vision-language models ( Ojha et al., 2024 ; Koutlis and Papadopoulos, 2024 ) , and reconstruction techniques that measure discrepancies between original and reconstructed images ( Karageorgiou et al., 2025 ) . However, most detection algorithms follow a data-driven approach, typically training on datasets generated using COCO captions ( Corvi et al., 2022 ) . Current benchmarks primarily focus on distinguishing between different generative architectures rather than evaluating performance across diverse content types. This creates limitations when detection systems encounter content that differs from their training distributions. Recent work has demonstrated that incorporating synthetic images collected “in the wild” from social media platforms can significantly improve detection performance ( Konstantinidou et al., 2025 ) , suggesting that the semantic content of synthetic images affects detectability. 3. Methodology Figure 1 . Overview of our automated harmful content generation pipeline. Starting from a set of captions, we use an LLM to transform them into unsafe prompts across unsafe categories. Then we use these unsafe captions as prompt to T2I models to generate potentially unsafe content. A flowchart diagram showing the research pipeline from left to right. It begins with a dataset of safe captions, flows through an LLM transformation step that branches into three unsafe content categories, then continues to multiple T2I generation models, and concludes with evaluation components including automated moderation tools and human assessment. We devise a systematic pipeline to evaluate the harmful content generation capabilities of T2I models at scale. Our approach leverages LLMs and T2I models to simulate realistic attack scenarios where malicious actors aim to use open models to generate harmful imagery. The pipeline serves two primary purposes: (1) mimicking human behavior in how potentially unsafe content could be crafted effortlessly using public datasets and open LLMs, and (2) providing an automated framework to assess harmful content generation capabilities at scale, enabling comprehensive evaluation across multiple models and content categories. Threat Model. We consider a realistic threat scenario in which a malicious actor has access to a consumer GPU and seeks to generate harmful visual content at scale. This actor does not require specialized expertise, jailbreaking techniques, or adversarial prompt engineering. It suffices to use an open-weight instruction-tuned model that complies with harmful instructions and iteratively refines a system prompt until the outputs meet their requirements. On the defender side, we consider the practical safeguards currently deployed by platforms: moderation APIs that flag harmful content and synthetic image detection algorithms that identify AI-generated imagery. Our evaluation pipeline is designed to systematically stress-test both the attacker’s generation capability and the defender’s detection robustness within this scenario. 3.1. Prompt and Image Generation Pipeline We begin with a collection of captions that serve as a starting point rather than generating prompts from scratch for two reasons. First, using diverse starting points as “seeds” increases the variability and realism of the resulting unsafe prompts, as they reflect different real-world entities and events. Second, the original safe prompts serve as a natural reference set for comparative analysis, allowing us to assess whether models exhibit equal capabilities in generating high-quality harmful versus benign content. To assess harmful content generation risks, we systematically transform original captions into unsafe prompts targeting categories of content that pose significant safety concerns. The transformation process uses category-specific prompting methodologies that instruct the LLM to create visually descriptive scenes incorporating harmful elements. We validate that our transformed prompts contained harmful content, as intended, using multiple specialized text classification models. The system prompt designed for this purpose is presented in Table 1 . This was iteratively refined through experimentation until the generated prompts were considered satisfactory by the authors. Each design element addresses specific issues identified during prompt generation testing. The requirement for explicit vocabulary emerged from observations that euphemistic language was less effective at bypassing safety mechanisms. The constraint against extravagant vocabulary prevents the generation of overly artistic or cinematic descriptions that might reduce the directness needed for effective unsafe content generation. Evaluation Framework Our evaluation addresses the central research question: How successfully can current T2I models generate harmful content when prompted appropriately? We employ a multi-level assessment approach that quantifies both attack success rates and the effectiveness of current detection mechanisms. To assess whether images generated from unsafe prompts actually contain harmful content, we employ pretrained content moderation systems. However, given documented limitations in automated detection systems, we conducted a human evaluation study using stratified sampling across caption types and generation models to establish reliable ground truth labels. Annotators were informed that all images were AI-generated. For each image, annotators rated five harm dimensions – sexually explicit content, stereotypes, violence/gore, self-harm, and hate speech – using a four-point scale: no , mild , moderate , and extreme . Ratings are guided by two dimensions considered jointly: the graphicness of the depiction (how explicit, severe, or detailed the harmful content is) and the apparent intent to depict or promote that content. The latter is particularly relevant for categories such as self-harm, stereotypes, and hate speech, where the same visual elements may carry very different meaning depending on context. In addition to the harm dimensions, annotators rated each image on a realism scale ( N/A , no , potentially , likely , yes ), reflecting how convincingly the image could be mistaken for a real photograph, combining rendering quality with scene plausibility. Full annotation guidelines, including per-category level descriptions, are provided in the Appendix. This enabled us to quantify the success rate of harmful content generation and the gap between current automated safety measures and actual harmful content detection capabilities. Beyond detecting harmful content, we assess the quality and prompt adherence of generated images using image quality assessment metrics. This quality assessment addresses whether models retain their generative capabilities when processing harmful prompts or output quality is reduced. Since T2I models achieve state-of-the-art performance on safe content generation benchmarks, we use images generated from original safe prompts as our reference standard. We employ two human preference metrics: ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023b ) , a BLIP-based ( Li et al., 2022 ) model that fuses image and text features via cross-attention and an MLP head to produce a scalar score reflecting joint perceptual quality and prompt adherence; and Human Preference Score v2.1 (HPS) ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , a CLIP ViT-H/14 ( Radford et al., 2021 ) model fine-tuned on large-scale pairwise human preference annotations, which scores an image-prompt pair by their learned embedding similarity. Both metrics output a single scalar quantifying how well a generated image matches its prompt and overall image quality according to human preference. Additionally, we evaluate synthetic image detection (SID) algorithms to assess their performance on explicit content. We test both standard detection models trained on benign datasets and “in-the-wild” variants trained on datasets containing explicit content. This analysis examines whether the semantic content of synthetic images affects detectability, addressing potential data drift issues when detection systems encounter content distributions different from their training data. 3.3. Implementation Details We use the Visual News dataset ( Liu et al., 2021 ) for safe prompts and focus on five categories of harmful content: sexually explicit material, violent imagery, harmful stereotypes, hate speech and self-harm. These categories were selected because they are frequently used as examples of unsafe content ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ; Qu et al., 2023 ) . As detailed in table 2 , we employ category-specific instructions for the five harmful content types. We employ Mistral-Nemo-Instruct-2407 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) for prompt transformation, because Mistral models have demonstrated capabilities in generating misinformation ( Vykopal et al., 2024 ) , and through empirical testing, it proved effective at producing sufficiently disturbing content for our evaluation purposes. For image generation five T2I models are used: Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0 , Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large (SD3.5) 2 2 2 https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-large , Flux.1 Dev 3 3 3 https://huggingface.co/black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev , AbsoluteReality 4 4 4 https://huggingface.co/Lykon/AbsoluteReality , and Juggernaut-XL 5 5 5 https://huggingface.co/RunDiffusion/Juggernaut-XL-v9 . For automated content moderation, we use ShieldGemma ( Zeng et al., 2025 ) , the OpenAI Moderation API ( OpenAI, 2022 ) and Amazon Rekognition ( Amazon Web Services, 2025 ) . For synthetic image detection, we evaluate four detection algorithms: SPAI ( Karageorgiou et al., 2025 ) , DeFake ( Sha et al., 2023 ) , RINE ( Koutlis and Papadopoulos, 2024 ) , and NPR ( Tan et al., 2023 ) . All four are initially trained on images created by Stable Diffusion using COCO captions, which do not contain explicit content. We additionally evaluate ITW variants of SPAI, RINE, and NPR, further trained on a dataset with images collected from social media confirmed to contain explicit content ( Chen and Zou, 2023 ) , as proposed in ( Konstantinidou et al., 2025 ) . Our human evaluation study relies on a sample of 1,500 images with balanced representation across categories and involved 8 participants (5 male, 3 female) for annotation, all of Greek cultural background. In total we received 6000 votes, with each image receiving at least 4 votes. Despite the limited scale, we consider the detection of explicit content sufficiently non-ambiguous that provides adequate ground truth labels across the evaluated harm categories despite the homogeneous annotator pool.
